cf.title: GIN jsonb_ops misses root strings in strict jsonpath queries

input.subject: GIN jsonb_ops misses root strings in strict jsonpath queries

verdict_reasoning: No objection survived at any level. The proposal fixes wrong query results: a jsonb_ops index scan misses a root string that a sequential scan returns, and two people hit it independently (messages #1 and #2). The fix changes query-side key extraction only, so existing indexes match without REINDEX. Message #3 reports that it was pushed.

brief.title: Fix GIN jsonb_ops lookups for root strings in strict jsonpath queries
brief.problem: A GIN jsonb_ops index scan returns no rows for strict-mode jsonpath queries that match a root string, such as @@ 'strict $ == "a scalar"'. A sequential scan returns the row. Users of jsonb_ops indexes with strict jsonpath get wrong results.
brief.proposed_design: gin_extract_jsonb() indexes a root string with JGINFLAG_KEY because a root scalar is stored as a one-element raw-scalar array. In strict mode, jsonb_ops__extract_nodes() searches for JGINFLAG_STR at the root, so the patch sets key_entry to GIN_TRUE for that case. Regression tests for @@ and @? are added to jsonb.sql.
user_visible_surface: Strict-mode @@ and @? queries on a jsonb_ops GIN index now return matching root strings; no syntax or API change.
author_claims: Existing indexes match after the fix; no REINDEX is needed.
Only strict-mode queries using jsonb_ops are affected.
make check passed all 239 tests; without the code fix only the two new indexed queries fail.
brief.thread_state: Shihao Zhong hit the same bug, reached the same one-line fix, and gave +1. Tom Lane replied that he pushed it with minor editorialization, so the CommitFest status "Needs review" is out of date.
unclear: The thread does not say which back branches received the fix, though the target is stable.
The patch does not say whether root non-string scalars (numbers, booleans, null) in strict mode are affected.
The thread does not say whether jsonb_path_ops has a similar issue or why it is safe.
Tom Lane's message does not say what the editorialization changed.

touch_points.label: backpatchability
touch_points.reason: The CommitFest target is "stable", and the thread does not say which back branches received the fix.

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)

questions: Which back branches received the fix, given that the CommitFest target is "stable"?
Do root numbers, booleans and null in strict mode have the same mismatch between gin_extract_jsonb() and jsonb_ops__extract_nodes()?
Does jsonb_path_ops return the matching root string for the same two strict-mode queries?
Should the CommitFest entry be marked committed, since message #3 says the fix was pushed?

committability.owner_note: Tom Lane pushed the fix with minor editorialization (message #3).
committability.liability: One changed line in the query-side key extraction of jsonb_ops, plus two regression queries. It adds no on-disk format, catalog, WAL or API surface to carry.
committability.author_follow_up: No sign either way; the fix was pushed four days after the report without a further message from the author.

priority.reason: The patch is a one-line wrong-results fix in jsonb_gin.c with two regression queries, and it affects only strict-mode jsonpath queries on jsonb_ops indexes. Message #3 says it was pushed, so the remaining work is to update the CommitFest entry, which still says "Needs review".

provisional_note: The code was not read, so the review could not check root non-string scalars in strict mode or jsonb_path_ops. Message #3 does not say what the editorialization changed.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add jsonb_translate(jsonb, from, to)
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Andrew Dunstan, Pavel Stehule, Peter Eisentraut
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds jsonb_translate(jsonb, from, to), and in v2 json_translate, which recursively replaces every value, including array elements, that exactly equals a given string with another string. The author meant it for mapping categorical or enum values deep inside a document, in the style of the Unix tr utility.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andrew Dunstan judged blind replacement of every instance of a string, regardless of context, to be a niche use and asked why it could not be an extension. Pavel Stehule suggested using JsonPath to say what to replace, and Peter Eisentraut pointed to json_transform in Oracle and the SQL standard draft, noting that json_transform and json_translate together might confuse users. The thread ends there, and the author later withdrew the entry.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Blindly replacing every
instance of a single string regardless of context seems at best a niche
use. Is there any reason not to make this an extension?

precedents_retrieved.title: Optimize JsonbContainerTypeName by reordering type checks
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch reorders the checks in JsonbContainerTypeName() so that the array and object bit checks run before the scalar check. The author argued that this avoids calling JsonbExtractScalar() in most cases and reported about 0.8% higher tps for jsonb_typeof().
precedents_retrieved.objection: David Rowley argued that one function call cannot change the speed of a whole query by a measurable amount. His test called the function 1 million times and found the patch 3.5% slower, and perf top showed JsonbExtractScalar using little CPU time. Andreas Karlsson added that scalars are not clearly less common, so the new order would slow some workloads while it speeds up others.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: It'll amount to a few dozen instructions for the function out of several 10s of millions, when you consider the cost of processing the entire query.

precedents_retrieved.title: Jsonb transform for pl/python
precedents_retrieved.summary: A set of extensions (jsonb_plpythonu, jsonb_plpython2u, jsonb_plpython3u) implementing a CREATE TRANSFORM for jsonb in PL/Python, mapping jsonb objects to dicts, arrays to lists, and numerics to Python Decimal via string conversion, and back. The transform works in both directions so functions can take and return jsonb as native Python values.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The reviewer objected that the third version turned unsupported Python objects such as set() into JSON strings instead of raising an error, asked for tests and errors for complex numbers and ranges, and reported that the tests failed on Python 3. The author sent no revised version after that review, and the commitfest manager returned the patch with feedback because it still needed work and had had no updates for more than a week.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
So this still needs more work.. I am marking it as returned with
feedback as there has been no updates for more than 1 week.

precedents_retrieved.title: allow mix of composite and scalar variables in target list
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch removes the PL/pgSQL parser check that rejects a row (composite) variable inside a multiple-item INTO list. With several targets, each target would take one output column, so a composite variable would receive one composite-valued column; record variables were left out.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that this makes a row variable mean one column in a multi-item INTO list but one column per field when it is the only target. That inconsistency would also limit later changes for backward-compatibility reasons. He asked for new notation that removes the ambiguity, and Robert Haas's support for the 1:1 matching did not settle it. The CF manager moved the patch on as needing a revised version, and Pavel Stehule answered with two new design options.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I'm fine with doing something where we add new notation to dispel
the ambiguity.  I don't want to put in another layer of inconsistency
and then have even more backwards-compatibility problems constraining
our response to the inevitable complaints.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fillfactor for GIN indexes
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add fillfactor as a storage parameter for GIN indexes, controlling how full pages are packed at index build time and, in later versions, the split ratio of posting-tree pages. Revised versions applied fillfactor only to posting trees and debated whether the default should be 100 (matching 9.4 index sizes) or 90 (matching btree).
precedents_retrieved.objection: No test results or benchmarks were provided showing that a fillfactor parameter improves GIN index performance, although an earlier reviewer had asked for them and got no reply. Robert Haas objected on that basis. The author agreed that no such benchmark existed and that he had no time to work on it soon, and asked for the patch to be rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There's only value in adding a fillfactor parameter to GIN indexes if
it improves performance.  There are no benchmarks showing it does.

precedents_retrieved.title: Pageinspect - add functions on GIN and GiST indexes from gevel
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Alexander Korotkov, Tomas Vondra, Ashutosh Sharma, Peter Eisentraut
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch moves the gevel module's functions for GiST, SP-GiST and GIN indexes into pageinspect, with tests and docs. The functions show whole-index statistics, print the tree and its stored objects, and estimate GIN value counts and query matches.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers said the functions read the whole index, while pageinspect inspects single pages, so the code belongs in a new extension or should be rewritten as page-level functions. Peter Eisentraut also found that the patch no longer compiled and that the stats functions returned one formatted text value where they should return a row with columns. The author planned a new contrib module but posted no new version, and the entry was returned with feedback after three weeks of waiting on the author.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The proposed patch uses a very different approach, reading the whole index,
not individual pages. Why should it be part of pageinspect?

precedents_retrieved.title: Predicate locking in Gin index
precedents_retrieved.summary: A GSoC 2017 patch adding explicit predicate locking to the GIN index access method for serializable isolation, placing page-level predicate locks on entry tree and posting tree leaf pages and copying locks on page splits. It also handled conflict detection when fast update is enabled.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewer Alexander Korotkov found the locking scheme redundant and asked for changes: lock posting tree leaves instead of entry tree leaves, apply page-level locks only when fast update is off, add in-code comments, and improve the isolation tests so they actually create posting trees. After his last review the thread had no updates for almost two months, and Michael Paquier marked the entry returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
This thread had no updates for almost two months, so I am marking it
as returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add jsonpath string method $.replace(from, to)
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Andrew Dunstan, "David E(dot) Wheeler", Peter Eisentraut
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a non-standard jsonpath string method, $.replace(from, to), which calls the internal implementation of the SQL replace() function on a JSON string value. The author planned more text methods, such as trim(), upper() and lower().
precedents_retrieved.objection: The thread does not state why the author withdrew the entry. David E. Wheeler noted that replace() is not in the SQL/JSON spec, and Andrew Dunstan objected that a future spec version could add an incompatible method with the same name, so he wanted non-spec method names prefixed or capitalized. Peter Eisentraut asked for a general way to call any suitable pg_proc function from jsonpath, and the author then began sketching that design instead.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The thing that bothers me about the original proposal
is this: what if we add a new non-spec jsonpath method and then a new
version of the spec adds a method with the same name, but not compatible
with our method?

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert the GinMaxItemSize calculation so that we fit 3 tuples per page.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert the GinMaxItemSize calculation so that we fit 3 tuples per page.
Reverted commit(s): Compress GIN posting lists, for smaller index size.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 36a35c55 changed the divisor from 3 to 6, for no apparent reason.
Reducing GinMaxItemSize like that created a dump/reload hazard: loading a
9.3 database to 9.4 might fail with "index row size XXX exceeds maximum 1352
for index ..." error. Revert the change.

While we're at it, make the calculation slightly more accurate. It used to
divide the available space on page by three, then subtract
sizeof(ItemIdData), and finally round down. That's not totally accurate; the
item pointers for the three items are packed tight right after the page
header, but there is alignment padding after the item pointers. Change the
calculation to reflect that, like BTMaxItemSize does. I tested this with
different block sizes on systems with 4- and 8-byte alignment, and the value
after the final MAXALIGN_DOWN was the same with both methods on all
configurations. So this does not make any difference currently, but let's be
tidy.

Also add a comment explaining what the macro does.

This fixes bug #12292 reported by Robert Thaler. Backpatch to 9.4, where the
bug was introduced.

roaster_notes.note: No precedent found: the retrieved candidates share keywords only, and the thread points to no earlier discussion of this bug. It is a narrow wrong-results fix in jsonb_ops strict-mode extraction, a second reporter reached the same fix (message #2), and message #3 reports it was pushed.

No objection from the standards and compatibility angle. The fix makes index scans return the rows a sequential scan already returns, and adds no syntax, GUC, catalog object or psql change. Existing indexes need no REINDEX and pg_dump output does not change. Not checked: root numbers, booleans and null in strict mode, and jsonb_path_ops; the thread does not cover either.

The fix changes only query-side key extraction in jsonb_ops__extract_nodes(), so existing jsonb_ops index entries match without REINDEX. It adds no WAL record, catalog change, on-disk format change or ABI change. A standby still on an older minor release keeps the old wrong results until it is updated, which is the existing bug rather than a new hazard.

The proposal has no privilege or exposure aspect. It changes which GIN key a strict-mode jsonpath query looks up for a root string, so an index scan returns rows a sequential scan already returns. It adds no object, privilege, function or setting, and it does not change what a user can read through RLS, column privileges or leakproofness. It adds no new memory, lock or worker cost. The fix was already pushed per message #3.

This is a one-line bug fix for wrong query results in jsonb_ops GIN lookups. It adds no new state, GUC, API, on-disk change or hot-path cost, and needs no REINDEX. Tom Lane, a committer who knows the area, pushed it (message #3), so the area has an engaged owner. From the maintenance and fit angle there is nothing to object to. Not checked without the code: whether root non-string scalars in strict mode, or jsonb_path_ops, have the same mismatch.

This is a wrong-results bugfix in jsonb_ops GIN lookups, and no existing feature, setting or extension gives correct results for these indexed queries. Avoiding the index or using jsonb_path_ops changes query plans or index choice, so it is not a substitute for fixing the bug.

This is a wrong-results bug fix, and two people hit it independently (messages #1 and #2). A fix for wrong query results needs no further evidence of demand, and the change adds no surface or hot-path cost. It was pushed in message #3.
